analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in American National Bank and Trust Company against Corico. Mr. Egan, you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please be the court. Perhaps the best way to start is by telling you, in contrast to what preceded your lunch, what this case is not about, and then to proceed to tell you what it is about. But it's not about the so-called standing requirement articulated by a majority of the judges in the Second Circuit, which implies and indeed requires a prior criminal conviction, either under RICO or under the predicate offenses. That issue was not addressed by the parties in the Seventh Circuit, nor was it addressed by the Seventh Circuit. The second facet of the Sedema case has certain comparable aspects to it, but is by no means the same, or do we necessarily adopt and follow the position taken by counsel on our side of that case. Now let me tell you what our case is about. First, in response to your position of the Second Circuit. I need not take that position, Justice White. I suppose if you asked me whether a prior criminal conviction was required, I'd have to answer you. But I think the analytical line that you will find in our briefs, in contrast to that on the so-called racketeering or RICO injury, as opposed to the standing issue, is quite different. Okay. And to respond initially to a question that you raised this morning, Justice White, we believe that this is a statute that indeed can and should be interpreted by this court. And we think that that task can be carried out within the four corners of the statute itself. The facts in this case are much like the hypotheticals that Justice Powell posed to counsel this morning. Now, this is a business dispute between a lender and a borrower. The lender, in this case, is currently, with its parent, the First National Bank of Chicago, the largest bank in the Chicago metropolitan area. The borrower was a businessman. Loans were made by the bank to this businessman. And in connection with those loans, the contract between the parties specified that they would be keyed to the so-called prime rate, which is alleged in the complaint to be the rate of interest charged by the bank to its largest and most creditworthy commercial borrowers for 90-day unsecured commercial loans. It is alleged that that contract was breached and that the bank, in fact, charged a greater rate of interest than it should have. This litigation is brought by the borrowers against the bank, against the bank's then-parent, which was a large commercial finance company named Walter E. Heller, which was then listed on the New York Stock Exchange, and by Ronald Grayheck, an executive vice president of the bank. The complaint sounds, with the exception of RICO, like the kind of thing that you find in any state court in the land today. A suit for a breach of contract, a claim that the bank breached an alleged fiduciary duty to its borrower, and a claim under an Illinois consumer statute that grants one attorney's fees. The RICO claims that are involved are under 1962C, relating to the conduct as opposed to the acquisition and maintenance. The district judge, on our motion, dismissed the complaint for failure to plead a RICO injury. An appeal was taken to the Seventh Circuit. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district judge and concluded that, I'm quoting, a civil RICO plaintiff need not allege or prove injury beyond any injury to business or property resulting from the underlying acts of racketeering. In other words, to go back to the discussion in which you were engaged with counsel this morning, the position of the Seventh Circuit, which was unanimous, and the court indicated no interest in holding a hearing on bank, or rehearing on bank, was simply that all you require are two predicate acts under 1961 and proximate causality, which is basically automatic, and an enterprise. Effectively, what the Seventh Circuit... You need something besides the two predicate acts to... No. An enterprise or not? No, Your Honor, you do not. Not under the Seventh Circuit? Not under the Seventh Circuit's analysis. The Seventh Circuit, I think, made it abundantly clear what they were doing. They were effectively reading 1962C out of the... and 1962A and B by implication, although the case here relates only to 1962C. It is our position that that interpretation of the statute is unwarranted. The standards to which this court must adhere in interpreting a statute are well known. They're spelled out in O'Hasco v. Silver. They require, one, an examination of the language of the statute, two, a plain meaning of the statute, not contrary to legislative intent, and three, no policy reasons not to follow that plain meaning. The statute, at least superficially, seems to be somewhat complex. As a matter of fact, in one of the other legal cases that the Seventh Circuit has decided, it is described as a treasure hunt. But we submit that it is not all that complex once it is read as an integrated whole. What is required in the first instance is a violation of one of the two predicate acts? Now, there was a good deal of discussion this morning about two acts alone being sufficient under RICO. I would suggest to the court that while that issue is not necessarily one that you need addressed, the definitional section of RICO does not define a pattern of racketeering activity as at least two acts of racketeering activity. It says it requires at least two acts of racketeering activity. It can reasonably be inferred, it seems to me, that you're dealing with a threshold without Congress having addressed at what level the pattern of racketeering activity or the number of predicate acts rises to the necessary status for purposes of concluding that you do indeed have a pattern of racketeering activity. Having satisfied 1961 in whatever fashion, you must then go to 1962C. 1962C states, it shall be unlawful for any person employed by or associated with any enterprise engaged in or activities of which affect interstate or foreign commerce commerce, excuse me, to conduct or participate directly or indirectly in the conduct of such enterprises' affairs through a pattern of racketeering activity or collection of unlawful debt. Now, that middle ground, the one that must be hurdled before one gets on to the injury issue, is what is ignored by the Seventh Circuit's decision. And we submit it is erroneously read it out of the statute. The net effect, as I mentioned a moment ago, is that I, as the aggrieved victim, if you will, of a so-called racketeering injury, need only establish two acts of mail fraud taking the liberal reading of racketeering, pattern of racketeering activity, and I've stated a RICO claim. Mr. Egan, a moment ago you said that the Seventh Circuit had read out what you referred to as the middle ground. Would you state what the middle ground is? The middle ground is step two, Justice Rehnquist. It's 1962C. It's the substance of offense. Judge Cudahy... Did you make this argument on the Seventh Circuit? We did not make this precise argument, Your Honor, and... So you're not, you're not, you're not attacking, challenging the Seventh Circuit's decision on the basis that you were presented below? I won't, I would say we are not challenging it on a different basis, Your Honor. What happened in the interim was the Seventh Circuit came down with its decision and after the case was argued in the Seventh Circuit but before it was decided the Sedema Trilogy came down. The argument that we made in the Seventh Circuit implicates the very same point I'm making here, namely that the statute had to be read as an integrated whole. The cases at that juncture, including the district court decision from which the appeal was taken, adopted the so-called racketeering injury really in a void without any analysis of the relationship between 1962C, which is a substantive provision, and the injury. In any event, the net result now, in contrast to the net result in Sedema, is that the floodgates are truly opened. if the Sedema approach is accepted by this court, particularly the prior criminal conviction, it seems to me that the floodgates are probably effectively closed. If the so-called... Closed or... Closed, Your Honor. Tightened up. I would think that the practical impact of requiring the prior criminal conviction of either the predicate acts or of RICO itself would be effectively to cut off. Yes, but the Sedema also... Didn't the Second Circuit also... They had a decision on the causation, too. They... Well, they dealt with it in terms of standing, and their approach to the meaning of a RICO injury was a, quote-unquote, injury of the type that RICO was calculated to reach. I know. That's a very subjective test, Your Honor. I know. We are not advocating that subjective test. But I think to the extent that the court opts to accept it, that our position is certainly vindicated, but on a different analytical basis. That requires something other than a reading of the four corners of the statute, Justice White. In a sense, it's the length of the emperor's toe or the mindset of the district judge. And I think one thing that's become abundantly clear in the large number of district court decisions that precipitated my trip here today is the fact that philosophically the district judges are all over the map. And indeed, the circuits are as well. They are very uncomfortable, I think, with some of the same questions that were raised, certainly the use of the terminology racketeering and others. And this has impacted their approach to interpreting the statute. Mr. Egan, what again is it? As I understand, the Seventh Circuit says you need the finding of civil guilt and the predicate offenses plus causation. Now, what more is it that you think 1962C requires? 1962C, by its very terms, requires that after you have an enterprise, that the enterprise be either conduct, or the person, conduct the affairs of that enterprise. In other words, run it. In other words, getting back to what you justices were asking this morning, isn't this statute really calculated to take care of the person who goes out with illegal gains and acquires a business, or someone who uses illegal gains to maintain a business, or lastly, someone who steps in and conducts the business, runs the business. Through. Through a pattern of... Through a pattern of racketeering activity. But you must run the business. You have to conduct the affairs. This is not dealing with incidental involvement, and in a sense that gets you back to the point that Justice Powell was making this morning and the implication of mail fraud. Well, is your client a... It's a bank, and it's a subsidiary of another bank? At the time of the operative events here, it was a subsidiary of a commercial finance company that was listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Today, it's a subsidiary of First Chicago Corporation. It was sold in the interim period. Could it be said to have been conducting the affairs of its parents? I think that, metaphysically, I have some problems with that. Judge Cudahy disagreed with us. We took the position, although Judge Decker at the trial level had disposed of the case only on the motion to dismiss. We had argued the enterprise person issue as well. In the Seventh Circuit, we raised again the enterprise person issue. Judge Cudahy accepted our argument in terms of the need for there to be a separate person separate from the enterprise, but concluded that, yes, indeed, in response to your question, a subsidiary could conduct the affairs of its parent. So you're saying what's missing in this case is proof of conducting the affairs of an enterprise? Allegations sufficient, Your Honor, to satisfy pleading requirements that, indeed, either American National conducted the affairs of its parent by charging a higher interest rate than it agreed to. I mean, that's the essence of this thing. This is about as far removed from mail fraud as you'll get. Indeed, the action, the original action in the pendent state counts didn't even contain a common law fraud claim. Well, the question that you presented for review here was whether a civil claimant must suffer damages merely by reason of the defendant's commission of the prescribed defenses without more. That's right. Or rather by the reason of the defendant's acquiring or conducting in a better... You don't... You think that... You think this question subsumes what you're arguing now? No, Your Honor, I don't. That's precisely my point. My point is that what the Seventh Circuit did was read the language that you'll find there acquiring, maintaining control of an interest in or conducting the affairs of an enterprise through. I mean, Justice White's question was directed to whether you think the question you presented for a review fairly subsumes the point that you are now making. Yes, I do. Mr. Egan, can I ask you, I still have the same problem I think Justice Rehnquist focuses on in 1962C. Assume that the complaint alleges that you made a lot of loans and that's part of the affairs of the bank is to make loans and that you did so by repeatedly making false representations as to what your major customers were getting, your prime rate, and therefore you repeatedly committed mail fraud or telephone fraud or something like that. Why then would that not be a pattern of activity, a pattern of racketeering activity through which you conducted the affairs of the enterprise? My position on that, Justice Stevens, would be that that is no different than any other loan we make. We determine whether we're going to require collateral, we determine the term of the loan. Yeah, but you don't regularly and routinely make fraudulent statements in making your loans, I'm sure. No, Your Honor, and while it's not a record we did in this case either. But that's what's alleged. If, in fact, you repeatedly and regularly made fraudulent misrepresentations and mailed them out to satisfy the mailing requirement, I really don't quite understand why that doesn't satisfy the definition under your analysis of the statute. Well, I think that perhaps I can best respond to that by giving the court an example of an instance, and these are reported cases, in which you did have conducting the affairs of an enterprise in a fashion that did pass muster, and indeed one of them, ironically enough, was the example that the Seventh Circuit used in Schacht versus Brown, which is one of the cases that's routinely cited by the people on the other side of this issue, and indeed one that troubled Judge Cudahy when he addressed our argument in the Seventh Circuit. In that case, the Seventh Circuit specifically found that the accountants and the insurance holding company facilitated the maintenance of the business, that is the insurance company, holding company, well beyond the point that it would have been able to do so by reason of fraudulent reinsurance agreements and misstatements of its financial condition. I think that goes to the essence of conducting one's business. I think the making of, or the determination, along with another laundry list of things of what rate you're going to charge someone an interest is not conducting the affairs. The business of banks and making loans and charging interest, and I don't, if you're, I would think that you're really running your business when you make loans and collect interest, aren't you? That's certainly one facet of your honor, but I don't think that goes to the essence of running your business. In Bennett versus Berg, for example, in a circuit case, the court concluded that the owner of a retirement home had routinely defrauded people who bought retirement contracts, that afterwards they had conducted the affairs of the retirement home in a fraudulent manner and continued to build money from these people. I think that those examples come much closer to the conduct. I think the conduct is something much more inherent than the determination of an interest rate that you're going to charge a borrower. But, Mr. Egan, it's not, as I understand the complaint, and you correct me if I'm wrong, they're not just saying you charged too high an interest rate, they're saying that you fraudulently, in other words, you made certain misstatements about what the prime rate was and then charge it on the basis of that. Isn't that right? I go back to what Justice Powell said this morning. We said we charge interest rate X and we in fact charge interest rate Y. They say that's fraud, I say it's a breach of contract. Well, of course, if you're right, you don't even have to reach the RICO issue then. There's no fraud at all. That would only occur as a matter of proof or to be developed in the course of discovery. They say we told you we would charge you X or we would use X as a base, which would result in a charge lesser than the one they claim we charged. I think that's about as common a contract type dispute as you're going to get. Certainly going to win the case without ever getting to these questions as Justice Stevens says. That's small consolation, number one, I think, to a national bank that is named in a RICO case. Justice Marshall alluded to a laundry list of very prestigious names in American business. It's a dubious distinction to be added to that list and I don't think that that's a burden that should be imposed on someone. It's a dubious distinction to be indicted too sometimes, I guess. And a lot of people have been indicted and still win their case. They're going to have to prove that you committed crimes if they win. That's true. The burden of proof was something that was addressed this morning. That's an interesting and open issue. They allege that your client's conduct was criminal. It seems to me I take it what you were saying is that this is somewhat like the case where a contractor gives a figure on a project and then performs and at the end of the line says that wasn't a bid, that was an estimate and I have to charge you more. So you've got merely an argument over what the contract was and if so whether there was a breach of that contract. And you don't want to go through this long process if you can avoid it to establish that. That's correct, Chief Justice. I think this is a classic example of the type of case that doesn't involve RICO. And as a matter of fact it's a classic example. Don't we have to assume for purposes of decision that the complaint alleges your client committed at least two felonies? I mean I know it's very unpleasant to make those assumptions for a very dignified company but that's the kind of problem we have to deal with. Yes, that's correct, Your Honor. It comes before you on a motion to dismiss. But as Justice O'Connor pointed out this morning the import of what you do here impacts many things beyond the sensitivities of the American National Bank. And really it is that global issue that I've tried to address my remarks and not to a parochial but very important interest to my client. Namely, based upon whatever standard the court articulates is a cause of action stated. It seemed to me you answered my question about 1962C by saying well it really was nothing more than an ordinary business transaction. And my question is if by reason of a series of felonious misrepresentations you have charged excessive rates why doesn't that constitute conducting business through a pattern of racketeering activity? And I'm really not sure of your hand. In a sense I think where we part company is on your determination of how integral to use the word we use in our brief the assessment of the rate of interest to be charged a customer is. I sense that you think that is material to be the interest rate of any charges is not the essence of its business? It's certainly an important consideration but I don't think it's the essence. What is the essence of it? Well the essence of its business is a myriad of things it's a determination of the initial credit worthiness of a customer it's a determination of whether you will require collateral from a customer it's a determination of what the discount rate will be how many points you're going to charge a customer on the front end whether this is going to be a term loan at a fixed rate or whether it will float will it float on a day by day basis will it float on a month by month basis there are a myriad of elements that go into it but I'll relate to Lenin You certainly would get out of this case an awful lot sooner than you would under the second circuit's approach Well under the second circuit's approach frankly I mean wholly aside from the predicate crimes point If the second circuit's approach I'm not talking about the prior criminal conviction but the injury of the type Rico was calculated to reach or to be adopted you would have a very very subjective test I think that my ability to get out sooner rather than later would be the reaction of a district judge who was running on an open field But your submission would be a cleaner way a surer way out Well I do not approach this as I said to just a student a moment ago You would avoid a lot of litigation But not only for my client your honor for others the numbers are somewhat staggering This is a pretty good example as I said of the kind of case that from my view and the view of my client doesn't belong in a Rico courtroom but the ABA task force report on Rico which was just released within the last couple of weeks and I believe has yet to be finally approved has some very interesting and impressive statistics 77% of all of the cases filed under Rico all of the cases that they've been able to determine the database obviously is not as broad as you would like involve securities violations or frauds in a commercial setting only 9% of the cases are true hardcore kinds of criminal cases and I sensed What would you say a hardcore kind of criminal case now if Illinois makes it a criminal offense to fraudulently represent something and damage somebody else would you say that's a hardcore kind of crime a felony yeah yes I would say that's a hardcore kind of crime but there is no such Illinois statute the only statute that they're proceeding on here is mail fraud and I don't have to tell this court how broad one writes as a prosecutor in the area of mail fraud yes it is it is has that ABA task force report been filed here no your honor we obtained a copy of it from some of the committee members I believe that others had access to it I notice a reference in at least one of the amicus briefs to some of the material that it contains it is luminous is it a public document yet I am confident that the ABA would make a copy available to the court Mr. Chief Justice we don't ask for these things we wait until someone presents them we can certainly make an application to file the document with you it may be of some assistance may I ask Mr. I gather you doesn't accept the prior conviction requirement does it we don't address it your honor I don't think that the prior conviction requirement can fairly be read into the statute now but of course the two predicate offenses have to be proved by the plaintiff and the issue of the burden of proof is an open one on that well that's what I wanted next to ask you what do you think the burden of proof should be I think the burden of proof should be the burden of proof in a criminal case beyond a reasonable yes I do as a matter of fact Judge Cudahy while he didn't give us much specifically left that question open and I think it is an open question and you say that I take it because the consequences of the proof on the burden are the same as in a criminal case precisely I'd like to reserve the few minutes I have remaining Mr. Hartunian Mr. Chief Justice may it please the court petitioner's argument in this case really amounts to a request to imply certain requirements of proof in place of the absence of the words that Congress could have used had it chosen to impose such requirements the words of section 1962C which govern this case are very clear any person violates RICO whenever he conducts or participates in the conduct of the affairs of an interstate enterprise through a pattern of racketeering activity which is defined as several predicate acts but those words are clear enough but petitioner petitioners say that that is not enough they say he must be a manager and then in the reply brief they shifted back to saying well it's okay if he's a low level person I suppose upon being confronted with the fact that this court has already construed the word conduct in other settings to mean low level people it does not have to be a boss or a manager or a supervisor and now Mr. Egan comes before you and tells you again that it must be some kind of managerial function involved when the pattern of racketeering activities occurred in it's interesting that the petitioners say that if it is a non-managerial person that person may still violate the act if his activities had some quote integral relationship and with the management of the enterprise and they say that that means the activities were the means by which the enterprise is being managed to quote from their brief that's interesting because what that apparently means is that in order for the activities to come within the act the activities have to be directed by the management of the enterprise or blessed by the management of the enterprise those requirements don't appear in the act and what they lead to is what occurred to me last night is amounting to a variation of the Nuremberg defense because according to petitioners a defendant can become exonerated for his activities if he can demonstrate that he was not acting under orders that's a bizarre kind of an approach to the statute and it's a very strange kind of an interpretation to seek particularly where what we're talking about when we discuss the enterprise and its affairs is not whether the enterprise is guilty the only issue in which the concept of the enterprise is implicated is whether the person was guilty of whatever it was that Congress said was so evil as to bring it within the penumbra of this act Mr. Hartunian if an employee of for example a bank conducted a pattern of fraudulent activity such as you've alleged here but only for the purpose of putting the money in his own pocket and not going into the bank's coffers would that meet the statutory requirement since I think the test is and I think it's clear the test is whether the frauds were committed in the course of transacting bank business those facts are absent from the hypothetical as presented but if the person was engaging in some kind of fraudulent activity which was bank business then clearly there's no reason to exonerate him well as I posed it it would be a bank employee who conducted this activity for his own profit not the bank yes he's playing his own game I understand but the question is not whether he benefited the enterprise the question is whether his criminal conduct occurred in the course of conducting or participating in the affairs of an interstate enterprise and the reason for that goes right to the question of why did congress impose an enterprise requirement why did congress discuss such a concept as an enterprise what's your answer to justice o'connor's question I believe that there's it depends on what which of two sets of facts are also involved if the person committed the fraud for example in the making of loans bank business then he is guilty because there is a sufficient nexus between what he's doing and the bank's interstate affairs and the bank is also liable that's a different question we're not even addressing it and it's not an issue in this case whether the enterprise is liable is really a matter that has nothing to do with any of the considerations we're talking about that has to do in my opinion the answer to that lies in normal respondeat superior principles in this case who is for 1962 c purposes who is the person and who is the enterprise there is an individual and heller international both of whom are persons whom we claim were persons who engaged in the enterprise known as American National Bank in another count we claim that American National Bank was a person that took part in the affairs of the enterprise known as heller international kind of a mutually interchangeable yes who committed the felonies in each instance the person alleged to have committed the felonies conduct was the person it was Mr. Greyhack and heller with respect to the affairs of a and b and in the other count it's a and b that committed the alleged felony while taking part in the enterprise of heller that that is the way it must be in other words you don't have a single theory of who the real culprit is you're sort of pleading in the alternative it is really pleading in the alternative obviously we cannot recover on both what what is your would you tell me again relating back to Mr. Higgins point about 1962 c just precisely what are the two predicate acts that you rely on mail fraud I know you said mail fraud but what did they do they say they didn't do anything but charge you too high an interest rate what do you say they did to put it very simply they lied about what their prime rate really was does that mean they're charging other customers a different rate that's right prime rate is an important benchmark which relieves both sides particularly the borrower of going shopping if he knows what the rate of interest is at which his bank is lending money to Chrysler he may very well say to himself well that's good enough for me this week and then when the bank says to him well we'll charge you one and a half percent over the best rate at which we're charging that week and we'll let you know what that is and he says fine I accept that they send him a bill saying this week our prime rate is ten percent you owe us a point and a half more than that here's your bill for interest at eleven and a half percent he pays it trusting them he doesn't know that's a lie they're really charging eight percent that's really the right assume assume the facts are as you're now tell me again who has committed the crime there are three people you've named an individual and two corporations the bank is the one who mailed you that information who committed the crime well the person who engaged in the lie committed the crime the just the fellow in the office who mailed out the notices he or the corporation on whose behalf he's acting committed it to well you see in a statute like this it's very helpful to know as precisely as we can whom it is that you say committed the criminal predicate acts and I have difficulty understanding exactly whom you're charging I think the easiest way to crystallize it is in the case of the person there is a named person an individual named in this complaint who we say was a person who committed the predicate acts while engaged in the affairs of an enterprise just taking that for the moment because it's the simplest to view he committed felonies he is the person we're suing he is the person against whom we are seeking a judgment when we discuss the enterprise whose affairs he was allegedly conducting we are referring to someone who is not being sued for purposes of that count so it is the person who committed the felonies the person who committed the male fraud does that answer the question well I think I understand what you're saying right congress could easily I gather you haven't had discovery yet that's probably part of the answer well we haven't had discovered but it unsettles me a little to think that that's part of the reason because I think the theory upon which the complaint is brought which is important to analyze what the statute means doesn't require any discovery but what the statute says is that certain persons are liable criminally or civilly and whether that liability attends depends in part not only on these other requirements of whether the predicate acts were violated and whether there was a pattern connecting those predicate acts but also to what extent was he engaging in the business of an interstate enterprise and the reason for that I think is that congress is establishing a nexus between the between the criminality and interstate commerce that was obviously of great importance to congress before getting to that though I just want to mention quickly that congress could easily have used the words petitioners say belong in this statute easily they're words familiar to all of us all lawyers and all members of congress manage supervise direct those words are absent from the statute had congress wanted to insist on any such element they could easily have used those words they could have used the phrase substantial relation to or integrally connected with but did not if you're addressing now an issue that was addressed by the court of appeals no well do you think it's an issue that's subsumed within the question presented in the cert petition I do not well I would think you might suggest that that is the case rather than just argue with it we did so in our brief well I know but I haven't heard you suggest it now and are you ever are you ever going to address the issue that was presented in the cert petition yes I intend to spend another moment just talking about the breadth of the statute because instead of using words of constriction words affording defenses and as a matter of fact worse than that if petitioners are correct these would impose requirements on the prosecutor in the first instance and upon the plaintiff as a necessary element so it's not just a matter of defense but instead of using terms of constriction congress used terms of breadth in every instance they use the phrase any person employed or associated by so employees can violate the act persons associated means persons completely outside the organization entirely directly or
